text: This is NodeSlide. It starts with one question — what presentation should we build? You bring an idea, a structured spec, or evidence, and it becomes a reviewable deck. Not a stack of static images.
You type a brief, in plain language. The brief drives the deck — there is no template underneath.
And this is a real deck. An outline rail on the left, the slide canvas in the middle, and an inspector on the right. Presenter notes travel with every slide.
Everything on a slide is a typed element. Select the headline — it is addressable and editable, not flattened into a picture.
The inspector is where the trust lives. Versions keeps revision history — you can compare snapshots and restore an earlier one.
Evidence keeps citations attached to the elements they support. And it is honest about its limits — it checks attachment and disclosure, and says plainly that it does not independently verify facts.
Trace shows one auditable run — the provider, the work performed, and validation. Where cost was not measured, it says not recorded, instead of printing a number it does not have.
Editable, versioned, evidenced, traced. That is what it means for a deck to stay editable.
